guide.orbitalis.arc_foundry.text:
The arc foundry melts two ingredients into an alloy.

It's crafted from 4 iron ingots, 3 copper ingots, 1 heating element and 1 redstone.

Place it against a generator and put the ingredients in the two blue slots, in any order. The result comes out in the orange slot.

Recipes:
- 1 iron ingot + 1 coal = 1 steel ingot (10 s, 6,000 FE)
- 4 aluminum ingots + 1 lithium ingot = 5 aluminum-lithium ingots (15 s, 15,000 FE)

If it says "Not enough energy", refuel the generator. "Output full" means the orange slot needs emptying.
guide.orbitalis.arc_foundry.title: Arc Foundry
guide.orbitalis.automation.text:
Machines accept hoppers and pipes from other mods.

A hopper pointing into a machine inserts whatever the machine accepts: recipe ingredients, or fuel for the generator.

A hopper underneath only takes what's in the output.

So a chest of coal hooked to the generator with a hopper keeps it running.

Power uses the FE standard, so cables and generators from other mods work too.

guide.orbitalis.conduits.text:
Conduits link your machines at a distance, so they no longer need to touch. There are four of them.

The power cable is a dark sheath with copper collars. 2 copper ingots with 1 redstone in the middle, in a row, make 6 cables. Its strands light up and pulse when current flows.

The liquid pipe is a thick glass tube in a steel cage. 2 steel plates with 1 glass block in the middle, in a row, make 6 pipes. Stained glass works too. It carries water, RP-1 and liquid propellants, and you can see the liquid flowing inside.

The gas pipe is a thin glass tube with brass rings. 2 glass blocks with 1 copper ingot in the middle, in a row, make 6 pipes. Stained glass works too. It carries gaseous hydrogen and oxygen between the electrolyzer and the liquefiers. Hydrogen swirls through it in red, oxygen in blue.

Lay them end to end and they connect on their own, to each other and to machines. Two different kinds of conduit won't join, and a pipe refuses what isn't meant for it. Gas won't go into a liquid pipe.

Conduits store nothing. Whatever a machine pushes in arrives at the other end straight away.

Power is shared equally between the machines on a network, and several generators can feed the same network.

For fluids, the first block that accepts is filled before the next. An empty tank takes any liquid, so give each liquid its own network if you're filling several tanks. Going to the launch pad, though, a single pipe is enough for every propellant.

Against a machine, the tube ends in a fitting and a collar in its colour. A long straight run has no joints and reads as a single tube.

A machine pushes what it makes, but a tank pushes nothing. To empty one, sneak and right-click the pipe touching it with an empty hand. The collar turns orange and striped, and the pipe pulls 2,000 mB per second into the rest of the network. In this mode it delivers nothing to the blocks it touches. Do the same again to switch it back.

The data cable is a thin black cable with turquoise dots. 2 aluminum plates and 1 redstone make 4 cables. It carries neither power nor fluid. It links control screens to what they display: launch consoles, tracking stations, tanks.
guide.orbitalis.conduits.title: Cables and Pipes
guide.orbitalis.crewed_flight.text:
The crew capsule is a 2,800 kg payload that goes under the fairing at the design computer. It needs the "Crew Capsules" technology and includes the cabin, the heat shield, the parachutes and the escape tower.

Once the rocket is on the table, right-click the cabin to climb aboard. Right-clicking anywhere else on the rocket opens the pad screen. When you get out, you end up on the boarding gate, back to the rocket. As long as it's on the ground, sneak to climb down.

On board, the launch key (Jump by default) opens the launch sequence, the same as at the console. You run it yourself, from fuelling to clamp release. The first to climb in is the pilot, seated up front, and only they have the controls. Two crew members can sit behind. The cockpit screen is on the ceiling and shows the mission clock, altitude, speed, trajectory and system status. The windows are on the sides.

The capsule rises with the rocket. What happens next depends on the launcher:
- on an atmospheric flight, it falls straight back;
- on a suborbital flight, you get a few seconds of weightlessness at the top;
- on an orbital flight (9,400 m/s of delta-v), you stay in orbit until you decide to come home (see "Space").
Then comes re-entry. Below 450 m, the air has slowed the capsule enough to arm the parachutes (Jump by default). They then open on their own at 140 m. Without them, the capsule crashes. In automatic mode, the flight computer arms them for you. You can't leave the capsule in flight.

If the launcher fails, the escape tower pulls the capsule off the rocket. Again, arming the parachutes is up to you, and quickly if it happens close to the ground.

On the ground, sneak to get out. Sneak and right-click the landed capsule to pick it up, it's reusable. The first crewed flight to space earns 150 research points, the first one to orbit 300, as long as you come back.

An uncrewed rocket can also carry a capsule. It's a test flight, and it comes back the same way.

There are three capsules. The Mk1 "Scout" has three seats, a dial panel and a navigation globe ("Crew Capsules" technology, 2.8 t). The Mk2 "Horizon" has four seats, three big screens and a touch console, with no stick ("Rendezvous and Docking" technology, 3.6 t). The Mk3 "Odyssey" has four seats, three screens, a big ceiling panel and a stick ("Lunar Lander" technology, 4.5 t). The fourth crew member sits in the middle, behind the pilot, on a step.
guide.orbitalis.crewed_flight.title: Crewed Flight
guide.orbitalis.cryogenics.scene.1: Place the electrolyzer against a water source, or empty a water bucket into it.
guide.orbitalis.cryogenics.scene.2: Hydrogen leaves on one side, oxygen on the other: place a liquefier on each side.
guide.orbitalis.cryogenics.scene.3: A tank against each liquefier collects the liquid propellant. Every machine must be powered.
guide.orbitalis.cryogenics.text:
Liquid oxygen and hydrogen are made in two steps.

1. The electrolyzer splits water into two gases. It's crafted from 4 steel plates, 1 glass, 2 copper ingots, 1 bucket and 1 redstone.

Placed against a water source, it fills itself. You can also empty a bucket into it. 100 mB of water gives 200 mB of hydrogen and 100 mB of oxygen, in 1 second, for 1,600 FE.

2. The cryogenic liquefier cools a gas until it turns liquid. It's crafted from 5 aluminum plates, 1 electric motor, 2 packed ice and 1 redstone.

100 mB of gas gives 50 mB of liquid in 2 seconds. That's 2,000 FE for oxygen and 3,200 FE for hydrogen.

Facing the electrolyzer, hydrogen comes out on the left (red mark) and oxygen on the right (blue mark). So you need a liquefier on each side, or a pipe leading to one.

Don't forget to power every machine, with a generator touching it or a cable.

Gases travel in gas pipes and liquids in liquid pipes. Between the electrolyzer and the liquefiers you need gas pipes, and after them, liquid pipes.
guide.orbitalis.cryogenics.title: Oxygen and Hydrogen
guide.orbitalis.energy.scene.2: Open it and add fuel: coal, wood, a lava bucket...
guide.orbitalis.energy.scene.3: Place a machine against it: energy flows straight into it.
guide.orbitalis.energy.scene.4: A generator shares its energy between all the machines touching it.
guide.orbitalis.energy.text:
Machines run on power, measured in FE.

The combustion generator makes it. It's crafted from 5 iron ingots, 2 copper ingots, 1 heating element and 1 redstone.

1. Place the generator.
2. Put your machines against it, or connect them with cables (see "Cables and Pipes").
3. Put fuel in the red slot: coal, wood, a lava bucket...

It makes 20 FE per tick, and one coal gives 32,000.

The green gauge on the right shows its 20,000 FE buffer. When it's full, the generator stops burning, so nothing is wasted.

The small screen shows its state: "Generating", "Buffer full" or "No fuel".

guide.orbitalis.engineering.text:
The skill tree gives your agency technologies, which is to say knowledge. The engineer's workbench turns that into hardware.

It's a drafting table two blocks by two, one block high. It's crafted from three steel plates, two iron ingots on each side and a crafting table in the middle. Right-click it to open its four sections: engines, tanks, payloads and launchers.

To study a part, you need its technology, researched in the tree, and the materials for a prototype, taken from your inventory. Those are mostly plates of the metal of the day, copper and redstone. The sheet compares what you have with what's needed. There's no luck involved. As soon as everything is there, the study succeeds, once and for all, for the whole agency.

A studied part can be used, both on a printed blueprint and on a rocket built by hand. Studying a launcher (its engines and tanks must already be studied) lets you print it ready-made at the design computer. So you can invent your own rockets from the parts alone, and only study a launcher to save time.

A study's dot is green when done, blue if it's possible now, orange if materials are missing, and grey if the technology or parts are missing.
guide.orbitalis.engineering.title: The Engineer's Workbench
guide.orbitalis.europa.text:
Europa, Jupiter's icy moon, hides under its ice shell a salty ocean bigger than all of the planet's put together. It's the best place in the solar system to look for life.

To get there, you need:
- the Europa ship ("Europa Lander" technology), a Mk3 cabin on a descent stage, under armour;
- a launcher that can reach Europa, which means 18,500 m/s. It needs a nuclear stage and its hydrogen tanks, for example four staged-combustion engines and twenty-four composite tanks, then a cryogenic engine and sixteen composite tanks, then a nuclear engine and thirty-two hydrogen tanks;
- an advanced suit with its radiation shielding module.

In orbit, press the departure key (Sprint by default) to plan the burn. At the mark, hold it and let go between 95 and 110% of the delta-v. Europa has no air, so the ship lands on its engine, like on the Moon. To leave, hold the launch key.

Europa is a shell of bluish ice, almost flat, streaked with long red-brown bands (the lineae, salts pushed up from the ocean) between ice ridges, with patches of jumbled, broken plates here and there. Gravity is 13% of the planet's, it's -160 °C, there's no air, and Jupiter fills a good part of the sky.

Jupiter bathes Europa in deadly particles. Without the shielding module on the suit's chest, you lose health every second you spend outside. The ship and bases protect you.

The cryobot ("Cryobots" technology) sits on the ice. Its heated head melts through the shell, and it goes down twenty kilometres to the ocean in ten minutes. Right-click it to see how far along it is. The first time an agency reaches the ocean, it finds traces of life. It's the biggest discovery in the game, worth 2,000 research points. Later dives earn 100.

The first landing earns 1,500 points, and the first steps 800. The planetary base kit works on Europa too.
guide.orbitalis.europa.title: Europa
guide.orbitalis.facilities.text:
The world hides space facilities. There are weather stations, research centres, observation centres and, much more rarely, control centres with their own launch pad. They show up in plains, savanna, desert, badlands, snow or on beaches, away from villages and behind a fence.

A weather station has an observation building, an anemometer mast and an instrument field. The bigger ones also have a radar tower under a radome and a shelter for weather balloons.

A research centre is a two-storey lab. The bigger ones have an engine test stand and a hangar.

An observation centre has a telescope dome, its control room and a small antenna. The bigger ones have a radio telescope.

A control centre has its firing room facing the pad, the assembly building with a rocket inside, a water tower, and the pad with its service tower.

About one in three is abandoned. The concrete is cracked, the cladding rusted, the windows broken, and the chests have already been looted.

The original equipment no longer works. Exhibit rocket parts, slabs, deflector, tower, consoles, screens, solar panels or floodlights only give back a bit of scrap when taken apart. Anything you place there yourself comes back normally.

Chests hold plates, ingots, rocket parts, sometimes a satellite, a spacesuit or a launch pad kit. You'll often find an archive blueprint, on a drafting table or in a chest, describing a ready-made rocket. Before building it, have the blueprint validated at the engineer's workbench, in the Archives tab. You need the technologies of its parts and half of its prototype. The launcher is then studied, and you earn research points along the way.

The blocks of these buildings can be crafted too: formwork concrete (with its slab and stairs), technical tiles, safety stripes, white, blue or rusted metal cladding, louvres, radome panels, curtain-wall glazing and antenna mesh.
guide.orbitalis.facilities.title: Space Facilities
guide.orbitalis.fuels.scene.1: Place the refinery against a fuelled generator.
guide.orbitalis.fuels.scene.2: Put coal in the blue slot: each coal gives 250 mB of RP-1.
guide.orbitalis.fuels.scene.3: Place a tank against the refinery: it fills by itself.
guide.orbitalis.fuels.text:
A rocket engine burns a fuel with an oxidizer, and together they're called propellants. You have three to start with.

RP-1 kerosene, a fuel that's easy to store.
Liquid oxygen, the oxidizer.
Liquid hydrogen, very efficient but hard to keep.

Fluids are measured in mB, and a bucket is 1,000 mB.

The refinery makes RP-1. It's crafted from 5 steel plates, 1 heating element, 2 copper ingots and 1 redstone.

Put coal in the blue slot. Each coal gives 250 mB of RP-1 in 5 seconds, for 4,000 FE.

Like every fluid machine, it pushes its output into the blocks touching it. Just place a tank against it.
guide.orbitalis.fuels.title: Fuels
guide.orbitalis.fusion.text:
Fusion propulsion is the best there is short of speculative technology. A plasma of deuterium and helium-3, held by magnets, heats hydrogen far more than a nuclear engine's reactor.

You need the "Fusion Propulsion" technology, which requires nuclear thermal propulsion and lunar helium-3, then the fusion engine, liquid hydrogen in hydrogen tanks, and helium-3 (see "Helium-3").

The engine has 2,500 s of specific impulse, almost three times the nuclear engine, and 900 kN of vacuum thrust, enough for a crew. It weighs 20 t and never lights on the first stage.

At the pad, on top of the hydrogen, it needs 1 mB of helium-3 per 20 mB of hydrogen, supplied by a helium-3 fuel port in the back left corner at the foot of the tower.

With a fusion stage, the Europa ship can go beyond Mercury on a lighter launcher than the nuclear one. For example, four staged-combustion engines and twenty-four composite tanks, a cryogenic engine and twelve composite tanks, then the fusion engine and sixteen hydrogen tanks.
guide.orbitalis.fusion.title: Fusion
guide.orbitalis.fusion_power.text:
The fusion reactor holds a plasma of deuterium and helium-3 in a ring of magnets. It's the biggest power source in the mod, 1,200 FE per tick, thirty times what a machine uses.

It needs the "Fusion Propulsion" technology.

Pipe helium-3 and gaseous hydrogen into it, on any face (hydrogen from the electrolyzer, not liquid hydrogen). It burns 2 mB of helium-3 and 20 mB of hydrogen every second, and sends its power to the cables and machines touching it. It stores up to 1,000,000 FE and shuts down when full. Right-click it to see its status.

The Casimir chamber makes exotic matter. Between two mirrors almost touching, the vacuum itself digs out negative energy. Put an ender pearl in it, and a minute and 480,000 FE later it comes out as exotic matter, the key to the warp drive.

A single reactor is enough to run three Casimir chambers.
guide.orbitalis.fusion_power.title: The Fusion Reactor
guide.orbitalis.helium3.text:
Helium-3 is a rare isotope of helium. The solar wind has been depositing it for billions of years in the Moon's regolith, which nothing shields. On the planet, the atmosphere and magnetic field stop it. It's the ideal fuel for fusion, because it gives off almost no neutrons.

It needs the "Lunar Helium-3" technology, which comes after planetary bases.

The helium-3 extractor is a rotary kiln that heats regolith to around 700 °C. Feed it lunar regolith or, better still, ilmenite ore (mined with Silk Touch), which holds four times more gas. A block of regolith gives 10 mB of helium-3 and 50 mB of hydrogen, and an ilmenite ore 40 mB of helium-3. Helium-3 comes out on the left, hydrogen on the right.

The machine works anywhere, on the Moon as on the planet, as long as you bring it regolith. It takes a lot, so store helium-3 in a tank for fusion propulsion.
guide.orbitalis.helium3.title: Helium-3
guide.orbitalis.index.hint: Pick a chapter. Arrow: animated demo (drag to rotate, scroll to zoom).
guide.orbitalis.launch.text:
1. Build. Print the rocket's blueprint at the design computer, put it on the table of a working pad, then place the blocks it shows. Right-clicking the deck with no block in hand places a whole layer. The rocket forms with the last block.

2. Set up. Right-clicking the table with the rocket stands it up on the pad. The pad must be formed, big enough for its mass, and its tower taller than the rocket. To take it back, sneak and right-click the table with an empty hand, or use the recovery remote within 48 blocks.

3. The launch sequence. It's shown on the left of the mission control screen, and on board, the jump key opens it. Its steps run in order, one click each. Nothing is left to chance. Each thing you forget always has the same consequence.

- Fill valves. Open them and fuelling runs from the tanks hooked up at the foot of the tower, RP-1 first, then the cold propellants (1 mB per 10 kg). The gauge takes at least fifteen seconds or so to fill. At 100%, click again to close the valves, or the pressure builds up. Without a full load, the engines will cut out in flight. A solid rocket doesn't need this.
- Pressurisation. It lasts two minutes and stops the cold propellants from boiling off. Without it nothing lights, and if it drops, part of the cold propellant goes with it.
- Arms and walkway. Retract them. Once the arm is retracted, nothing more goes into the rocket and nobody can board. If you forget them, the rocket rips them off as it leaves and tears itself open.
- Water deluge. It uses the pad's water reserve, filled through the water fuel port in a corner at the foot of the tower, with a pipe or buckets. Without the deluge, the flames break deck slabs.
- Ignition. Thrust builds up over three seconds.
- Release the clamps, only at full thrust. Too early and the rocket falls back onto its table. The clamps hold for twelve seconds, after which the engines are cut and part of the propellant is lost.

While the rocket is held down, "Cut the engines" stops everything.

The sequence carries on in flight. Its list shows the steps of this flight, and each lights up when its moment comes. You have at least five seconds to command it.

The flight. The rocket follows its trajectory on its own. On board, you don't fly it, you make the decisions. Each one appears in the middle of the screen with its key (the space bar by default, changeable in the options under "Orbitalis: piloting") and a draining gauge. Press before it runs out.

Two or three times per flight, at random, a gust or a drifting nozzle pushes the rocket off course. The screen then asks you to hold a key for a few seconds, or to press it in time. If you make it, the rocket gets back on course. If not, it veers off (the stall alert sounds), loses speed and, in dense air, strains its structure, before the computer straightens it out.

A flight lasts 20 to 50 seconds depending on the destination and the number of stages. Between decisions, the screen shows the next one and how long until it comes. On the left, a timeline shows the climb and the flight's steps, and a line at the bottom gives speed, altitude, apoapsis and stage. At liftoff, the view switches outside and slowly circles the rocket as long as you leave the mouse alone. M opens the orbit map. An uncrewed rocket is commanded the same way from the console.

The flight computer can help. Click "Assist", at the top right of the screen, to change its level (only on the ground). In assisted mode ("Gyroscopes" technology), it throttles down and cuts the engines itself. In automatic mode ("Flight Computers"), it does every flight step and closes the valves once fuelling is done. The ground sequence is still yours. Each flight step done by hand earns a 2 research point bonus.
- Throttle down (liquid fuel), between the 3rd and 8th second. Otherwise the structure fails at max Q.
- Separate the stage, at each empty stage. Otherwise nothing drops it, the rocket drags it along with engines out, and it's lost.
- Jettison the fairing (uncrewed), once in space. Otherwise the payload stays shut in and the mission fails.
- Cut the engines (orbital flights), in the last five seconds. Otherwise the orbit is missed and the mission fails.

A missed step can't be made up, and a flight missing one earns nothing. Only the flight computer can do them for you, at the assist level you picked.

4. Follow the flight. The console, the screen walls and the cockpit screen show altitude and speed. At the end, the agency gets its research points. There's a bonus the first time it reaches a milestone (10 for an atmospheric flight, 30 for space, 100 for low orbit...), and 5 points per sounding rocket payload sent to space. A satellite goes into orbit, a station module deploys, a capsule comes back down.

The launcher itself is lost after the flight.

Accidents. A lost rocket doesn't just vanish. It breaks up section by section, each according to what it holds: a fireball for kerosene, a white cloud and a flash for cold propellants, a shower of sparks for solid fuel. The shockwave hurts and throws back anything close. The nearest pad blocks are destroyed and the blueprint shows what to rebuild, but the table and the deflector always hold. Around it, the ground is scorched, a few fires start and debris rains down. Pick it up, it smelts back into steel. The damage depends on the rocket's mass and propellant. A sounding rocket chips a few slabs, a fully loaded heavy launcher flattens the deck and the foot of the tower. A rocket lost in flight explodes in the air, and its wreck lands further away, along the trench. The server option "Rocket accident damage" can limit this damage to the pad, or turn it off.

The pace. Each operation takes a few seconds (the valves open, pressure rises, the arm swings away), and nothing else can be commanded meanwhile. Before ignition, running a poll is a good idea. Each station answers go or no-go, and if any says no-go, ignition is held. The answer is valid for 90 seconds. Nothing forces you. Without a poll, the ignition button always works, even if fuelling isn't done, and the rocket will blow up in flight when its engines cut out.

By technology. A solid rocket has no fuelling and no pressurisation. A turbopump engine (kerosene) also needs chilling through the arm, which only lasts two minutes. A staged-combustion or hydrogen launcher must also switch to internal power. The list only shows the steps your rocket needs.

Overpressure. Once fuelling is done, close the valves. If they stay open while the pad's tanks keep pushing, pressure builds up in the rocket. The relief valves vent, the valve line flashes red, then the alarm goes off. After thirty seconds, the tanks burst and the rocket explodes on the pad. Once the valves are closed, pressure drops in a few seconds. In automatic mode, the flight computer closes them itself.

Pad tests. In the "Go / No-Go" window of mission control, you can run three tests whenever you like, with or without a rocket, as long as nothing is lit. The deluge runs for eight seconds and uses a quarter of a real deluge's water, the arms swing out and back, and the alarm sounds. A test deluge doesn't protect a real liftoff.

Mission control. Its screen brings everything together. On the left, the launch sequence, which you can run from here. On the right, a 3D model of the pad, animated like the world: the arms swing away, the engines light, the rocket rises. Rotate it with the mouse and zoom with the scroll wheel. A tab switches to the navigation map, which the screen also does by itself at liftoff. Below, the telemetry. The "Go / No-Go" button opens a window with the stations, the poll and the pad tests. "Abort launch" cuts everything while the rocket is held down.

The navigation map. The console and the screens show the terrain in blocks, seen at three-quarter view, like the atlas. In flight, the map pulls back as the rocket climbs, until it shows the whole planet. The rocket follows its trajectory. It climbs straight, gradually tips toward its heading and races for the horizon, and an orbital launcher then circles the globe. Behind it you see the path flown and its shadow on the ground, ahead, the planned path in dashes with the stage separations, up to orbit insertion. The "View" button in a corner turns the map a quarter turn.

The atlas. The "Atlas" button, at the top of the mission control map, opens the world map full screen. Drag to move around, and zoom with the scroll wheel, from single blocks to a whole region. The "View" button at the bottom changes the angle, and a compass at the top right points north. From afar, each pad is drawn as a miniature. The cursor gives coordinates, altitude and terrain type, and markers show mission control, the pads and your position. Wherever someone has already been, the map shows the world as it is, buildings and trees included, even if the area is no longer loaded. Where nobody has gone, it shows the terrain the world will generate. A mission control only knows its surroundings, whose limit is dotted.

Layers. The "Layers" button at the bottom shows or hides three layers. Facilities shows the pads and their state (free, rocket and propellants, countdown, in flight), mission controls and tracking stations, even far away and unloaded, with their last known state. Flights in progress shows the ground track as a solid line, then its continuation in dashes, with altitude and distance flown. Danger zones shows, around a rocket on its pad, where the shockwave and debris would reach if it blew up, and under a rocket in flight, the corridor where its pieces would fall. Click a facility or the terrain to open its card, and the cross closes it.

The sky. Two more layers depend on your agency's satellites. With a weather satellite in service, the map shows the world's real clouds from above, with their shadows, grey and rainy when it rains. They fade as you zoom in. Around tracking stations, a green square shows the ground surveyed by observation satellites. Until the navigation constellation has four satellites, your position is only known to within a few blocks, and an orange circle shows it. At the bottom right, a line sums up the sky (weather and relay). Click it to expand weather, relay, navigation and observation.

The mission tablet. With the "Mission Tablet" technology, the tablet (6 aluminum plates, a display, a circuit board and a redstone) opens the atlas with a right-click, anywhere on the planet, as long as one of your agency's telecommunications satellites relays the data. The atlas is then centred on you, with a "via satellite" badge. Without a relay, or away from the planet, the tablet tells you so.

What the agency knows. On its own, a mission control knows 1,536 blocks around it. Each observation satellite in service adds 1,280 blocks, up to 4,096.

Markers. Right-click the map to place a marker your whole agency can see. Its card says where it is and who placed it. You can rename it (Enter to confirm, Escape to cancel) or remove it.
guide.orbitalis.launch.title: Launch
guide.orbitalis.launch_complex.scene.1: Right-click with the kit, then pick the size and the tower. The pad is previewed where you're looking, and the scroll wheel rotates it. Right-clicking the ground places the launch table one block up, and the blueprint appears.
guide.orbitalis.launch_complex.scene.10: Swap a frame block at the foot of the tower for a fuel port, one per propellant, and hook your tanks to it. The console must be at least 8 blocks from the table.
guide.orbitalis.launch_complex.scene.2: Under the deck, the flame deflector goes below the table, surrounded by the supports that will carry the slabs.
guide.orbitalis.launch_complex.scene.3: The deck goes in at table level. Leave the flame trench line clear.
guide.orbitalis.launch_complex.scene.4: The flame trench is a straight line of gratings from the table to the edge. The table turns them the right way by itself.
guide.orbitalis.launch_complex.scene.5: A lightning mast stands on each corner, with a floodlight just below its top. The two deluge rails frame the rocket, open in the middle to leave room for the boosters.
guide.orbitalis.launch_complex.scene.6: Start the tower with its utility column. It rises from the ground, against the deck, in the middle of the side facing the rocket.
guide.orbitalis.launch_complex.scene.7: Then the rest of the tower, five blocks wide: the frame, the stairs and landings (or the elevator shaft), and a railed platform on top.
guide.orbitalis.launch_complex.scene.8: The umbilical arm hangs from the utility column on the rocket side, and the boarding gate opens in the same face. The blueprint shows where they go.
guide.orbitalis.launch_complex.scene.9: With the last block in place, the blueprint disappears. Right-click the table to form the pad. If a block gets broken, the blueprint comes back to show what's missing.
guide.orbitalis.launch_complex.text:
A launch pad is built from a launch pad kit, made of a launch table and a sheet of paper.

Right-clicking with the kit opens its screen. You choose the deck size (5×5, 9×9 or 11×11) and the tower, with stairs or an elevator. The screen shows the mass and height of the rockets this pad can launch, the space it takes, and the blocks you need next to what you already have. Once confirmed, the launch table is placed one block above the ground.

The blueprint appears in the world right away, each block in place as a see-through ghost. The layers in progress are detailed and outlined in yellow, the rest is just a silhouette. You can place blocks one by one, or right-click the table (or any deck slab) with nothing in hand to place the whole yellow layer at once with what you're carrying. Block orientation doesn't matter, the table fixes it. Right-clicking the table tells you what's still missing.

Under the deck sit the flame deflector and the supports. On top come the slab deck with its flame trench, a mast on each corner, the deluge rails, and the five-block-wide tower on the side opposite the trench. The tower starts from the ground. Its utility column, in the middle of the side facing the rocket, carries the umbilical arms, and a railed platform caps it. All these blocks are solid, so you can walk on them.

In the stair tower, you go in through a side door and a spiral staircase climbs around the core to the top, one side per floor. Nothing overhangs it closer than four blocks.

In the elevator tower, you go in from the back into a car that fills the whole inside, three by three and three high. Right-click the car floor to open the floor panel. It stops at the ground and at every boarding gate. Right-clicking a boarding gate calls it. The shaft is enclosed, and the landing doors only open when the car is there.

A mast floodlight lights up to sixteen blocks ahead of it, but not its surroundings, and anything in the way cuts the beam. On a working pad, the floodlights turn toward the rocket and come on at night and during launches, and the mast beacons blink. Anywhere else, a floodlight is switched on by redstone.

Careful: from ignition until the rocket is high up, the exhaust burns everything at the foot of the rocket, on the deck and far along the trench. Keep your distance.

A two-flight staircase on the left side of the deck leads up from the ground.

Once the last block is placed and the sky above the table is clear, the blueprint disappears. Right-click the table to form the pad, provided your agency has the "Launch Pad" technology. The deck, masts and arms take on their finished look. If a block gets broken, the pad comes apart at once and the blueprint returns to show what's missing.

For fuelling, swap a frame block at the foot of the tower for a fuel port ("Tank Farm" technology). Right-click it to choose its propellant: kerosene, liquid oxygen or liquid hydrogen. You need one per propellant the rocket carries. Put your tanks against it or connect them with a pipe. As soon as a rocket is on the table, fuelling happens by itself, kerosene first, then the cold propellants, which slowly boil off while the rocket waits.

The boarding gate, three blocks wide and tall, opens in the utility column, facing the rocket. It's part of the blueprint, like the umbilical arm, so place it where the blueprint shows. As soon as a crewed rocket, or its blueprint, is on the table, the table moves the boarding gate up to the cabin's height. The staircase turns with it so that a landing always opens onto it. A walkway reaches from the arm to the rocket, and retracts fifteen seconds before liftoff.

For mission control, place a launch console 8 to 64 blocks from the table. Control screens ("Mission Control" technology) placed side by side form a big screen from three wide and two high. To link it, sneak and right-click the console, then right-click the screen wall.

With a tower block or a mast segment in hand, right-clicking a column you've already started places the block on top, like scaffolding.
guide.orbitalis.launch_complex.title: Launch Complex
guide.orbitalis.mars.text:
Mars is further than the Moon, and tougher.

The Mars ship is an 8 t payload ("Mars Lander" technology). It's a beefed-up lunar ship, with an entry shield, big tanks and engines. It goes under the escape tower, like a capsule.

You need a heavy launcher that can reach the Mars transfer, which means 13,000 m/s of delta-v. That's a bit more than for the Moon, with a heavier payload.

In orbit, press the departure key (Sprint by default) to plan the burn. At the mark, hold it and let go between 95 and 110% of the delta-v. The ship arrives high above Mars and enters its atmosphere. It's a hundred times thinner than the planet's, enough to slow the ship but not to land it.

The landing is up to you. At 170 m above the ground, the descent engine arms. Only two forces are at play: the engine's thrust, along the ship's axis, as long as you hold the step key (Jump by default), and gravity. Engine off, the ship falls. On, it brakes. Your attitude controls tilt it, and tilted, it slides sideways. The engine throttles itself. It brakes hard as long as you're coming down too fast, then holds a steady descent, without ever pushing you back up. Keeping it on the whole way gets you down, and cutting it at times saves propellant, which is limited.

From your seat, you can't see the ground under the ship, so land on instruments. The panel shows height, descent speed, drift, tilt and propellant. Below the attitude ball, a prompt tells you what to do: burn, let it fall, level out or cancel drift. The outside view (F5) helps too.

At touchdown, don't go over 6 m/s down, 5 m/s sideways or 25° of tilt. Beyond that, the ship breaks apart. In automatic mode, the flight computer lands for you.

On Mars, sneak to get out, in a suit. Gravity is 38% of the planet's. The ground is rust-coloured dust over brown rock, pitted with craters, under an ochre sky. The rock holds hematite, which gives iron. Bringing samples back earns research points, and the first landing is worth 900.

To come back, hold the launch key for three seconds on board. The ship lifts off and returns to the planet's orbit, from where you go home as usual.

Beyond Mars, it's probes that explore. Each launches like a satellite, on a launcher that can reach its target: Venus (12,900 m/s), Jupiter (16,000), Saturn (17,200), Titan (17,500), Europa (18,500) and Mercury (22,000). Chemical engines are barely enough anymore, you need an ion stage, a sail or a nuclear engine. Orbital probes (Venus, Mercury, Jupiter, Saturn, Europa) map their body. The Venus lander and the Jupiter and Titan descent probes dive into the atmosphere and measure it all the way down. Distant probes draw their power from a reactor core ("Radioisotope Generators" technology). The first mission of each type to each body earns a big bonus, bigger the further away it is.
guide.orbitalis.mars.title: Mars
guide.orbitalis.methane.text:
Methalox is liquid methane burned with liquid oxygen, as in Raptor engines. Denser than hydrogen and cleaner than kerosene, its big advantage is that it can be made far from the planet.

It needs the "Methane / Oxygen Engines" technology, which unlocks the methalox engine and the Sabatier reactor.

On the planet, it takes two steps:
1. The Sabatier reactor takes coal (or charcoal) and gaseous hydrogen. 800 mB of hydrogen and one coal give 400 mB of methane and 200 mB of water. Methane comes out on the left, water on the right.
2. The cryogenic liquefier turns it into liquid methane, 50 mB of liquid for 100 mB of gas.

On Titan, place the ice drill at the edge of a methane lake. It pumps liquid methane from every lake block within reach and pushes it into the tanks touching it. A bucket works too.

At the pad, a methalox rocket needs a methane fuel port, in the back corner at the foot of the tower, in addition to the oxygen one. Like oxygen, methane is loaded after kerosene.

Liquid methane is cryogenic and boils off outside a cooled tank, except on Titan, where it's -179 °C.
guide.orbitalis.methane.title: Methane
guide.orbitalis.missions.text:
Each mission has its own needs, in pad size, launcher power, and sometimes propellants or equipment. The design computer's catalogue has a launcher for each.

Sounding rocket (suborbital flight)
- 3×3 test pad, or 5×5 pad.
- A solid motor, a sounding rocket payload and a fairing.
- No propellant to load, the solid motor has its own.
- It goes above 100 km and earns 5 research points per flight, plus the first-flight bonuses.

Liquid-fuel test
- 5×5 pad, with tanks hooked up at the foot of the tower.
- Two pressure-fed engines and one tank.
- RP-1 and liquid oxygen.
- A chance to get fuelling right before aiming higher.

Satellite in low or polar orbit (experimental, weather, observation, telescope)
- 5×5 pad for a 125 t launcher. The telescope, at 11 t, needs a heavier one.
- Two stages and 9,400 m/s of delta-v.
- RP-1 and liquid oxygen.
- On the ground, a tracking station to follow the satellite and receive its data.

Satellite in medium or geostationary orbit (navigation, telecommunications)
- 5×5 or 9×9 pad, depending on the launcher.
- 11,850 m/s of delta-v, so a cryogenic upper stage.
- RP-1, liquid oxygen and liquid hydrogen.
- With too weak a launcher, the satellite is lost. The table warns you when you set the rocket up.

Crewed suborbital flight
- 5×5 pad.
- A crew capsule on a single stage.
- Board through the boarding gate and its walkway, or by right-clicking the cabin. Launch from the cabin (jump key) or from the console.
- The capsule comes back under parachutes, a little way from the pad.

Crewed orbital flight
- 5×5 pad.
- Two stages, 9,400 m/s with the 2.8 t capsule.
- A spacesuit to get out of the capsule.
- In orbit, the jump key prepares the return.

Space station
- 5×5 pad.
- Two stages, 9,400 m/s with the 3 t core module, launched uncrewed.
- A crewed orbital flight from the same pad then docks with it, and more modules extend it.
- The station deploys right above the pad, so always launch to it from that site.

Lunar flight
- 9×9 pad, 38-floor tower.
- Three stages, 12,550 m/s with the 6 t lunar ship. You need staged-combustion engines and large composite tanks. The catalogue example weighs 355 t and stands 26 blocks tall.
- RP-1, liquid oxygen and plenty of liquid hydrogen.
- A spacesuit.
- In orbit, the sprint key prepares the departure for the Moon.

In every case:
- the launch console goes 8 to 64 blocks from the table;
- fuelling happens by itself as long as the tanks stay hooked to the fuel ports;
- you can't launch in a thunderstorm;
- the pad screen (right-click the table or a slab) shows the allowed mass and height, and those of the rocket on it.
guide.orbitalis.missions.title: Which Pad for Which Mission
guide.orbitalis.moon.text:
Going to the Moon takes three things.

First, a lunar ship, a 6 t payload ("Lunar Lander" technology): a crew capsule sitting on its landing stage. It goes under the escape tower, like a capsule.

Then a heavy launcher that can reach the Moon, which means 12,550 m/s of delta-v. Small tanks won't do. You need the staged-combustion engine, twice as powerful as the turbopump engine, and the large composite tanks, four times bigger than the others. A launcher like that weighs several hundred tonnes, so plan for a 9×9 pad with its 38-floor tower.

Last, a spacesuit, because there's no air on the Moon.

After liftoff, you stay in free orbit. On the way out, a lunar ship doesn't dock with your station, it's only passing through. Press the departure key (Sprint by default) and the flight computer plans the trip to the Moon. At the mark, hold it and let go between 95 and 110% of the delta-v. The ship arrives above the surface and comes down on its engine, slower and slower, until it touches down. No parachutes here, without air they'd be useless.

On the Moon, sneak to get out. Gravity is only a sixth of the planet's, so you jump very high and fall slowly. The ground is regolith over moon rock, peppered with craters. Bringing samples back earns research points.

Moon rock contains ilmenite, which gives raw titanium, far more common here than on the planet. At the bottom of some large craters, there's still lunar ice. With a bucket, it gives water, which the electrolyzer turns into hydrogen and oxygen. Enough to make propellant on the spot.

Anything that works in a station works here too. Build a closed room (out of station hull, or any solid block), put an air generator in it and power it. You can breathe there without a suit, and it recharges. Solar panels give full power, as in orbit. Close the base with two doors in a row, opening only one at a time, to keep the air in. The planet hangs in the sky.

To come back, get back on board and hold the launch key (Jump by default) for three seconds. The ship lifts off and returns to the planet's orbit, or to your station. From there, you go home as usual, under parachutes.

The first Moon landing earns 500 research points, and the first steps 300. Don't lose sight of your ship, it's your only way home.

Before sending a crew, you can send robots. A lunar or Mars probe ("Robotic Probes" technology) launches like a satellite. If the launcher reaches the body, it goes into orbit and maps it. A robotic lander ("Landers" technology) actually sets down on the surface, about thirty blocks east of the point above the pad. Its coordinates are announced, and a crew can go and visit it. The first mission of each type to each body earns a big bonus (lunar probe 60, Mars probe 100, lunar lander 100, Mars lander 150), later ones a bit of science.

With the "In-Situ Resources" technology, the ice drill pulls water from lunar ice, placed on it or up to four blocks above. On Mars, the oxygen extractor pulls oxygen from the atmosphere. Both have their own generator and push what they make into the tanks and pipes touching them. The electrolyzer does the rest. Right-click to see their status. With the "Planetary Bases" technology, the planetary base kit builds, with a right-click on the ground of the Moon or Mars, a pressurised module (the same as in a station) with its airlock door. Module kits connect to it as in orbit. The first base on each body earns 80 points.

With the "Sample Return" technology, a lunar or Mars sample return mission launches like a probe. It lands, scoops up soil and sends its capsule back to Earth (Moon: 120 points the first time, then 25; Mars: 200, then 40). A crew can also do the job themselves. On site, right-click the ground with a sample container to take a bit of rock. Back on Earth, a right-click hands them to the agency lab (Moon: 150 points the first time, then 30; Mars: 250, then 50).

With the "Lunar Orbit Station" technology, the lunar station launches like a satellite, on a launcher that can reach the Moon. It settles into lunar orbit, shows up at the tracking centre and earns 10 points a day for 300 days, plus 150 points the first time.
guide.orbitalis.moon.title: The Moon
guide.orbitalis.ores.text:
Three ores generate in the Overworld.

Bauxite is common, between Y 32 and 112. A stone pickaxe is enough. It's where aluminum comes from.

Lithium is less common, between Y -32 and 48. Stone pickaxe as well.

Titanium is rare, between Y -64 and 16, and needs an iron pickaxe.

Each ore drops its raw form, which you smelt in a furnace or blast furnace to get an ingot. Fortune increases the drops.

Nine ingots of steel, aluminum or titanium make a storage block.

Its tower has 38 floors, and the whole thing covers 14×9 blocks, deck included.

The demo builds it piece by piece, in order. Step through it, rotate it and zoom with the scroll wheel. It shows an elevator tower, but the stair tower is built the same way.

guide.orbitalis.pad_sizes.text:
There are three pad sizes. The bigger the deck, the heavier the rocket can be, and the taller the tower, the taller the rocket can be, since it has to stay below the top. They're all built the same way (see "Launch Complex"), and the kit gives the exact block list for each size.

The 5×5 launches rockets up to 200 t and 24 blocks tall. Its tower has 26 floors and it covers 10×5 blocks. It's the starter pad, for sounding rockets, satellites and the first crewed flights.
The 9×9 goes up to 3,000 t and 36 blocks, with a 38-floor tower, on 14×9 blocks. It's the heavy launcher pad, for the Moon, Mars and high orbits.
The 11×11 goes up to 10,000 t and 44 blocks, with a 46-floor tower, on 16×11 blocks.

To change size or tower, right-click the table with another kit. The blueprint is replaced and shows what needs adding. There must be nothing above the table.

guide.orbitalis.research.text:
The skill tree holds all of your agency's research. Open it anywhere with K, which you can change in the game options, under "Orbitalis: piloting".

The Technologies tab has nine rows, one per field: propulsion, structures, avionics, ground infrastructure, satellites, crewed flight, stations, exploration and advanced propulsion. You progress from left to right. A green box is unlocked, a blue one can be researched, a dark one is still waiting on a prerequisite. Drag the view to move around.

Click a box to show its sheet on the right. It lists the cost, what it brings, its prerequisites (sometimes from another field) and the studies it opens at the engineer's workbench. The "Research" button, or a double click on the box, spends the points.

Research points are earned by playing. First steel ingot, first flight, first satellite, first steps on the Moon... The Objectives tab sorts them into six tiers and shows the ones you've already reached. Each one pays only once.

In multiplayer, an agency is a team (the /team command). Its members share their points and technologies. A player with no team has an agency of their own.
guide.orbitalis.research.title: Research
guide.orbitalis.rocket_assembly.text:
A rocket is drawn up at the design computer, then built block by block on its pad.

The design computer is a big console, three blocks wide and two high. Right-click to open it. The rocket is shown in 3D on the left, the stage editor on the right. Start from a known model (from the sounding rocket to the Mars launcher) or a blank sheet, pick the payload, then set up to three stages. For each one, you choose the engine and how many, then the tank type and how many. Engines that carry their own propellant (solid, hypergolic, ion) have no tank. Each stage shows its delta-v and thrust-to-weight ratio, and the whole rocket its mass, delta-v, propellants, destination and first problem. Only parts studied at the engineer's workbench are offered. The scroll wheel steps through a choice or a number.

"Print blueprint" gives you a rocket blueprint. It costs a sheet of paper and the chosen payload, which you must be carrying and which goes with the blueprint. Your agency must master every part of the launcher.

With the blueprint in hand, right-click the table of a formed pad that's big enough. The blocks to place appear above the table as models, layer by layer. Right-clicking the table tells you what's missing.

Each section has its block, in the middle. Parts place themselves. Right-click the matching model with an engine, a tank, an interstage or a nose cone, and the part slots in. Each block costs what the blueprint asks. The bay of a three-engine stage takes three, a tank section of a big rocket takes two, and on a slim rocket one tank spans two blocks (the second is free, but you need the part in hand). A removed block gives back what it cost. The payload bay, fairing, hull panels, cable raceway, flight computer, solid motor casing, cabin, roof and escape tower are crafted and placed like ordinary blocks.

When a rocket is waiting to be built, right-clicking the table opens the build screen. It shows the rocket as it stands, the placed blocks, the current layer, then what's left to gather piece by piece next to what you're carrying, any missing fuelling hookups and the payload on board. "Place layer" places the next layer, and "Place all" everything you can.

In the editor, the first stage can carry a pair of solid boosters ("Solid Boosters" technology). They burn with it at liftoff, add their thrust and delta-v, and drop off on their own once empty, with no step to command. On the pad, they stand on either side of the rocket, at right angles to the tower, up to seven tenths of the first stage's height. Each is built from its nozzle (the booster itself), solid motor casings and a nose cone.

Once the rocket is standing, the pad screen offers "Copy blueprint". Like printing, the copy costs a sheet of paper and the payload. It's handy for keeping a hand-built rocket and building it again elsewhere.

A heavy launcher is three blocks wide. Each central block is ringed with hull panels, with a cable raceway on the tower side, the extra engines around the first one, and the flight computer at the top of the last stage.

The rocket forms when the last block goes in. If you break one of its sections, it comes apart. Its blocks come back, except the one you broke, which drops to the ground, and the blueprint shows where to put it back. Sneak and right-click the table with an empty hand to take the rocket apart, and once it's dismantled, the same move takes the blueprint back.

After launch, the blueprint stays on the pad. You can build the same rocket again, or take it back to place another.

You can also build without a blueprint. On a working pad, stack an engine and its tanks along the table's axis, maybe an interstage and another stage, then finish with a payload bay and a nose cone, or a cabin with its roof and tower. With each block, the table shows what the rocket is worth (delta-v, destination, mass) and what it's missing. The more tanks a stage has, the more propellant it carries. Hand the payload to the table with a right-click. Once the stack makes a rocket, the table draws up a blueprint from it, and all that's left is to place what it shows, like the hull of a wide rocket or the fuel ports. Sneak with an empty hand to take that blueprint, and your invention can then be rebuilt like any printed one.
guide.orbitalis.rocket_assembly.title: Design and Build
guide.orbitalis.rocket_stats.text:
The design computer recalculates everything as soon as you change a setting.

Mass is the whole rocket, tanks full.

Thrust is the first stage's thrust at liftoff.

TWR is thrust divided by weight. It must be above 1 at liftoff, or the rocket won't leave the ground. Add engines or remove tanks.

Delta-v is all the speed the rocket can gain. It comes from the Tsiolkovsky equation, specific impulse × 9.81 × ln(full mass / empty mass). To raise it, use a more efficient engine, lighter tanks, or add a stage.

As a rough guide, you need about 1,700 m/s to reach space, 9,400 m/s for low orbit and 11,850 m/s for a geostationary transfer.

For the same volume, a tank holds almost three times less hydrogen than RP-1. The hydrogen engine is more efficient, but it needs more tanks.

The last line says what the rocket can reach, or the first problem to fix. Hover over the screen for each stage's details: propellant, dry mass and burn time.

At launch, the flight is worked out step by step from these numbers. The rocket feels its thrust, its weight and air drag. It gets lighter as it burns propellant, drops its empty stages, and an orbital launcher gradually tips over toward the horizontal. Liquid-fuel engines throttle down so as not to exceed 4 g. The screens show the flight sped up (altitude, speed, acceleration, active stage) with the mission clock in real time. Whatever propellant is left at orbit insertion is your margin.

The ion thruster ("Ion Propulsion" technology) and the solar sail ("Solar Sails" technology) are placed like engines on the last stage, without tanks. The thruster's xenon is loaded at the factory, and the sail needs no propellant at all. Their thrust is tiny. They can't lift off and only work in orbit, where they accelerate for months. So their delta-v only counts if the chemical stages reach low orbit on their own, and is then added to the rest. The ion thruster has a specific impulse of 3,100 s, ten times a chemical engine. The sail gives a fixed impulse, so the lighter the payload, the more delta-v. Neither is suitable for a crew, the trip would take months.

The nuclear thermal engine ("Nuclear Thermal Propulsion" technology) heats liquid hydrogen in its reactor, with no oxygen. At 900 s of specific impulse it does twice as well as the best chemical engine, and its vacuum thrust is decent. But it weighs almost four tonnes, and hydrogen alone is so light that it needs a lot of tanks. It's only for upper stages. A blueprint that puts it on the first stage is refused, since its reactor never lights above the pad. It only needs hydrogen when fuelling.
guide.orbitalis.rocket_stats.title: Statistics
guide.orbitalis.rolling_mill.scene.1: Place the rolling mill against a fuelled generator.
guide.orbitalis.rolling_mill.scene.2: Put an ingot in the blue slot.
guide.orbitalis.rolling_mill.scene.3: Five seconds later, a plate arrives in the orange slot.
guide.orbitalis.rolling_mill.text:
The rolling mill flattens ingots into plates. Plates are what rocket structures and tanks are made of.

It's crafted from 4 steel ingots, 2 iron ingots, 1 electric motor and 1 redstone.

Put an ingot in the blue slot, and a plate comes out 5 seconds later.

It makes steel, aluminum, titanium and aluminum-lithium plates. Each costs 2,000 FE, except titanium, which is harder and needs 4,000.
guide.orbitalis.rolling_mill.title: Rolling Mill
guide.orbitalis.satellites.text:
A satellite is a payload. At the design computer, it takes the place of the sounding rocket's instruments, under the fairing. If the flight succeeds, it goes into orbit and works for your agency.

Each satellite aims for a specific orbit, which the launcher must be able to reach:
- low orbit (LEO, 400 km) and polar orbit (SSO, 800 km): 9,400 m/s of delta-v;
- medium orbit (MEO, 20,200 km) and geostationary (GEO, 35,786 km): 11,850 m/s. The launcher drops the satellite on a transfer orbit and its own engine does the rest, just like for real.
If the launcher falls short, the satellite is lost. The rocket's tooltip and the launch table warn you beforehand.

The satellites:
- Experimental satellite (85 kg, LEO): 1 research point a day for 15 days.
- Weather satellite (700 kg, SSO): 2 points a day and weather forecasts, for 60 days.
- Observation satellite (1,200 kg, SSO): 4 points a day for 60 days.
- Telecommunications satellite (1,500 kg, GEO): relays the others' data continuously, for 120 days.
- Navigation satellite (1,000 kg, MEO): 1 point a day for 100 days. Four in service form a constellation, which earns a bonus.
- Space telescope (11 t, LEO): 12 points a day for 150 days.

The first satellite of each type earns a bonus. Watch the mass, since the heavier the payload, the less delta-v the launcher has. At the end of its life, a satellite stops working and must be replaced. Lifespans can be turned off in the server settings.
guide.orbitalis.satellites.title: Satellites
guide.orbitalis.shipyard.text:
No rocket could launch an interstellar ship. So it's built in orbit, at the shipyard attached to the station.

You need the "Orbital Shipyard" technology, which comes after the lunar gateway and fusion propulsion, and the shipyard module, brought on board.

From inside the station, right-click a wall with the module. It opens a glazed control room and, behind it, a cradle of beams 31 blocks long, open to space. It needs 13 blocks of width and height.

The console, facing the window, holds the ship's blueprint, a hull 29 blocks long with a ring 11 blocks across. Missing blocks show as ghosts, and the current section in detail. Place them by hand, or from the console screen with "Build section" and "Build all", which take the blocks from your inventory.

Each section is built, then fitted out. The warp core goes in the engine room (you need the warp drive), the ring motor on the ceiling, then four hibernation pods, eight grow trays under their lights, and the helm between two consoles. The pods and the core are two blocks tall but placed as a single item.

To finish, load the core with eight exotic matter with a right-click, then run the check at the helm. It tells you, system by system, what's still missing.
guide.orbitalis.shipyard.title: The Shipyard
guide.orbitalis.space.text:
A crewed orbital flight really takes you to space. Once the engines cut off, the capsule and its crew are in orbit, in vacuum, under a black sky.

In orbit there's no up or down. You float and move as if in water, swimming where you look, then drifting and slowly stopping. Jump to go up, sneak to go down, sprint to swim faster.

The capsule is pressurised, you can breathe normally inside. To get out (sneak), you need a complete spacesuit: helmet, chest, leggings and boots. If a piece is missing, it isn't airtight. The chest carries the life support pack, with ten minutes of oxygen, shown on the item like a durability bar. The helmet shows the remaining oxygen, the pressure and the seal on the left of the visor. Without a suit, or with an empty tank, you suffocate in a few seconds.

The advanced suit, white, is made of titanium around the pieces of the orange suit. It lasts a quarter of an hour and protects better, but above all, each piece takes modules. Right-click with a module to fit it to the piece you're wearing, or holding in your other hand, and sneak-right-click with the piece in hand to remove the last one fitted. The helmet can take the proximity map and the environment sensor, shown on the right of the visor. The chest takes an extra oxygen tank (ten more minutes) and thrusters for weightlessness. The leggings take shock absorbers.

The suit recharges while you sit in the capsule, and on its own once you're back on the planet.

To come home, right-click the capsule to get back in, then press the return key (Jump by default). The flight computer plans the braking burn and starts a countdown. At the mark, hold the key and let go between 95 and 110% of the requested delta-v. The capsule then re-enters above its pad and lands under its parachutes. Don't lose sight of it, it's your only way home.

Your agency's first spacewalk earns 100 research points. Without a crew, an orbital flight is just a test flight, and the capsule comes back on its own after two orbits.
guide.orbitalis.space.title: Space
guide.orbitalis.stations.text:
A station starts with its core module, a 3 t payload ("Station Modules" technology) launched uncrewed. If the launcher reaches low orbit, the module deploys on its own right above the pad. It's a padded, pressurised room three blocks across, with three windows, the docking port, the air generator on the ceiling, the terminal under the north window, a half-charged battery, a wing of five solar panels on the roof and an antenna.

To get there, launch a crewed orbital flight from the same site. The capsule arrives about thirty blocks away, lines up with the port, then closes in by itself, slowing down until contact. Stay on board during the manoeuvre. Once docked, sneak to go through the port, and you're inside, no suit needed. To leave, right-click the port from inside, then hold the jump key.

Right-clicking the terminal opens the station dashboard. It shows the layout, power (production, consumption, batteries), orbit, air, lab, greenhouse, crew, cargo and ships. The station goes around the planet in five minutes, a little over a third of that in shadow, and the header counts down the eclipse.

The air generator pressurises the whole enclosed volume around it, up to 4,000 m³, as long as it gets 20 FE per tick. A broken wall or a port open to space, and the air is gone in two seconds. Keep a suit within reach. Greenhouse plants recycle the air, and each planted tray saves the generator 2 FE per tick.

Everything in the station shares the same power grid. A solar panel ("Solar Panels" technology) gives 40 FE per tick in sunlight and nothing during eclipse. Whatever its neighbours don't use goes into the batteries (500,000 FE each), which everything else draws from. Plan enough to last through the eclipse.

Each module is crafted with its equipment, then taken on board, in your inventory or as launcher cargo, in which case it's delivered behind the port. Right-click a wall from inside to deploy it. The module is built on the other side, fully fitted, and the passage opens.
• Habitation: four bunks, four lockers and a terminal. An injured crew member rests on a bunk with a right-click and recovers.
• Laboratory: eight experiment racks. In orbit, with air and power (40 FE per tick), each rack runs one experiment per orbit, every five minutes, earning a research point.
• Greenhouse ("Closed-Loop Life Support" technology): eight grow trays for wheat, carrots, potatoes or beetroot. With power, a crop grows in just over two minutes. Right-click to harvest, and the tray replants itself.
• Logistics: eight cargo lockers, 216 slots in all.
• Cupola: a glass dome to watch the planet go by. The crew also observes planets and moons from there, and each cupola (two at most) adds one to the agency observatory's power.
• Airlock: two hatch doors. They open as you approach. The airlock equalises (air hisses, the light turns amber), the hatch rises and the light turns green, then it comes back down once the way is clear. The two doors are interlocked. While one is open, the other stays shut, and the station keeps its air.
• Power truss ("Large Solar Arrays" technology): a lattice truss, two wings of four panels and a battery, outside.
An extra core module makes an empty room.

All these blocks can also be placed one by one. Hull, lining, floor, ceiling lights, windows and closed ports are airtight. Air passes through grow trays and the lattice truss.

If you die in space or on another world, you wake up on the planet, at your bed or the world spawn.

Your agency's first station earns 250 research points, and its first experiment 50.
guide.orbitalis.stations.title: Space Stations
guide.orbitalis.storage.scene.1: The cryogenic tank stores 32,000 mB of a single fluid.
guide.orbitalis.storage.scene.2: When powered, it keeps liquid oxygen and hydrogen without loss.
guide.orbitalis.storage.scene.3: Without energy, these propellants slowly boil off. RP-1 is not affected.
guide.orbitalis.storage.text:
The cryogenic tank holds 32,000 mB of a single fluid. It's crafted from 6 aluminum plates, 2 insulation blankets and 1 glass.

Placed against the machine that makes the fluid, it fills itself.

Liquid oxygen and hydrogen are cryogenic, they have to stay very cold. As long as it's powered, the tank keeps them without loss for 10 FE per tick, and its screen reads "Active cooling".

Without power, it reads "Boiling off!" and loses 5 mB per second.

RP-1 and water don't need power. The screen then reads "Stable storage".

Hover over a gauge to see the fluid and the amount.

The modular tank is simpler. 6 steel plates and 2 glass make 2 blocks of 16,000 mB. Placed together, they merge into one square tank, from a single block up to 3×3 and 12 high, which is 1,728,000 mB. You can see the level through its windows, and right-clicking with an empty hand tells you what's inside.

It takes any liquid or gas, but only one at a time. Two tanks holding different fluids stay separate even when they touch. If you remove a block, the contents stay in the others, as long as there's room.

It isn't cooled, so a cryogenic propellant boils off at 2.5 mB per second per block. Think of it as a buffer, and keep the cryogenic tank for oxygen and hydrogen.

It doesn't push anything by itself. Empty it with a pipe in extraction mode (see "Cables and Pipes") or with a bucket.

A control screen placed against a tank, or linked with a data cable, shows its level. The same screen linked to a launch console shows the launcher and its pad, and linked to a tracking station, the satellites. Panels merge into one screen, up to 16×9. Sneak and right-click to switch to the next display.
guide.orbitalis.storage.title: Storage
guide.orbitalis.test_pad.text:
Your first sounding rockets don't need a tower. A test pad is enough.

In the launch pad kit, pick the 3×3 size. It's a plain platform: a flame deflector under the table, supports at the corners, eight deck slabs and a flame trench. No tower, no masts, no arm.

It only takes uncrewed solid-fuel rockets, up to 20 t and 8 blocks tall. A liquid-fuel rocket needs an arm to fill its tanks, and a crew capsule needs a gangway, so those need a 5×5 pad.

The test console is crafted from 3 steel plates, 2 iron ingots, 1 glass pane, 1 circuit board and 2 redstone. Place it at least 8 blocks from the table, and no more than 64. It only shows the launch sequence, with no map and no rocket sheet.

Once the pad is in service, build your rocket on it, open the console and work down the list: the Go/No-Go poll if you want one, ignition, then release the clamps when thrust reaches 100%%.
guide.orbitalis.test_pad.title: The Test Pad
guide.orbitalis.titan.text:
Titan, Saturn's big moon, is the furthest place you can land.

The Titan ship is a 7 t payload ("Titan Lander" technology, which needs the Mars lander and nuclear thermal propulsion). It's a four-seat Mk3 cabin inside an entry shell, with parachutes and a small ascent stage. It goes under the escape tower, like a capsule.

You need a very heavy launcher that can reach Titan, which means 17,500 m/s of delta-v. Chemical engines aren't enough. You need a nuclear thermal upper stage, which burns only liquid hydrogen, with its big, light hydrogen tanks. For example, three staged-combustion engines and sixteen composite tanks, then a cryogenic engine and twelve composite tanks, then a nuclear engine and twenty-four hydrogen tanks. Ion engines and sails won't do for a crewed flight, they push too little.

In orbit, press the departure key (Sprint by default) to plan the burn. At the mark, hold it and let go between 95 and 110% of the delta-v. The ship arrives high above Titan and goes in shield first. Titan's air is four times denser than the planet's. It slows the ship enough for its parachutes to land it, like the Huygens probe in 2005. Arm them as you would coming home (in automatic mode, the flight computer handles it). Without them, the ship crashes.

On Titan, sneak to get out, in a suit. You can't breathe there, the air is nitrogen and methane at -179 °C. Gravity is 14% of the planet's, so you jump very high and falls barely hurt. The ground is brown tholin sand, organic grains fallen from the haze, over water ice as hard as rock. Under the orange haze, you can't see far.

Below a certain height, the low ground is full of liquid methane. You can swim and sail in it like water, and scoop methane with a bucket. You can also drown in it, and you only see a few blocks. Anywhere but Titan, poured methane boils away at once. Water, on the other hand, freezes on the spot, so you can't pour it.

To come back, hold the launch key for three seconds on board. The ship lifts off and returns to the planet's orbit, from where you go home as usual.

The first landing on Titan earns 1,200 research points, and the first steps 700. The planetary base kit works on Titan too.

The flying drone ("Rotorcraft" technology) sits on the ground, and a right-click sends it to survey a site up to a hundred blocks away. It comes back on its own, recharges its battery for thirty seconds, then sets off again. Each new site earns 25 research points, and the first flight 150. On Mars, the air is so thin that it only makes forty-block hops, for 15 points.

guide.orbitalis.tracking_station.text:
The tracking station is a dish antenna. Place it under open sky and right-click it. The map shows the planet, the four orbits and your satellites, each going round at its own pace.

A science satellite produces data continuously and keeps it in memory for three days at most. Beyond that, the oldest is lost. The "Receive data" button turns it into research points, so drop by regularly.

With a telecommunications satellite in service, data comes in on its own, wherever you are.

With a weather satellite, the station shows the current weather and how long it will last. That's handy for timing a launch, since you can't launch in a thunderstorm.

Satellites belong to your agency. All your stations show the same thing, and your teammates see them too.

The console benefits as well. With a weather satellite, it shows the launch window and warns you when the weather turns. With a telecommunications satellite, it controls a pad up to 256 blocks away instead of 64.

The "Survey" tab shows what your observation satellites see, the ground around the station chunk by chunk, with its ores. One satellite covers a square five chunks wide, two cover seven, and three or more cover nine. Pick an ore in the list to show only that one, and hover over a square for its coordinates.

The "Observatory" button turns your satellites to the sky. With the "Tracking Stations" technology, pick a body and point your instruments at it. Each observation satellite counts for one, each space telescope for three, and only the telescope sees deep sky (nebulae, galaxies, the black hole). Each body is only visible at certain times, which come round again over the days: the Moon around full moon, Mars at opposition, a comet as it passes, deep sky in its season. Outside of that, the instruments stay pointed and wait, and the screen says when the window opens. The image builds up as you observe. Once the body is discovered, receive its image (you need to see the sky, or have a relay). It earns research points and the body goes into the catalogue.

Each discovery leads to others. The Moon leads to Mars and Venus, Mars to Jupiter, the Pleiades to deep sky. The catalogue collects your discoveries, a double page per body with its photo and its card. For a planet or moon, the card explains how to get there (distance, travel time, delta-v, gravity, atmosphere, temperature), which launcher to take, and what equipment to bring, technology by technology, showing what your agency already has.

guide.orbitalis.welcome.text:
Welcome to Orbitalis!

This manual follows the mod's progression, from the first ores to rockets. The easiest way is to read the chapters in order.

Your first goal is steel. To make it, you need ores, power and an arc foundry.

If JEI is installed, click an item to see its recipe.

Almost everything is crafted from components, parts that are only used for that. The first two are the heating element (copper, iron, redstone) and the electric motor (steel, copper, iron, redstone). They are enough for the foundry, the generator and the rolling mill. The rest come later: circuit board, flight processor, display, reinforced glass, LED lamp, insulation blanket, steel grating, photovoltaic cell, battery cell, inertial unit, optical sensor, radio transmitter, heat shield tile and CO2 filter. Their tooltip says what they are for.

observatory.orbitalis.body.andromeda.des: The great neighbour of our Galaxy: a trillion stars, 2.5 million light-years away. It is heading towards us, and the two galaxies will merge in four billion years.
observatory.orbitalis.body.comet.desc: A ball of ice and dust that returns every seventy years. Near the Sun it unfurls two tails: dust, curved and golden, and ions, straight and blue.
observatory.orbitalis.body.crab_pulsar.d: The remains of a star that exploded in 1054, recorded by Chinese astronomers. At its centre a neutron star spins thirty times a second, sweeping space with its beams.
Columns of gas and dust several light-years tall, in the Eagle Nebula. Stars are born at their tips, which the light of their neighbours slowly erodes.
observatory.orbitalis.body.europa.desc: A moon of Jupiter covered in ice, streaked with brown cracks. Beneath the ice lies an ocean of liquid water: one of the most promising places to look for life.
observatory.orbitalis.body.jupiter.desc: The giant of the solar system, with no surface, striped with cloud bands. Its Great Red Spot is a storm wider than Earth that has raged for centuries.
observatory.orbitalis.body.mars.desc: The red planet: iron-oxide deserts, giant volcanoes, ice caps. Its air, a hundred times thinner than ours, barely slows a spacecraft: a Mars lander touches down on its engine.
observatory.orbitalis.body.mercury.desc: The closest planet to the Sun, riddled with craters. Scorching by day, frozen by night; landing there takes more energy than reaching Pluto.
observatory.orbitalis.body.moon.desc: Our neighbour, three days away. Its dark basalt seas and craters keep the memory of the young solar system. A lunar module can land there.
A stellar nursery, 1,350 light-years away. At its heart four very young stars, the Trapezium, make all the gas glow: hydrogen in red, oxygen in teal.
observatory.orbitalis.body.pleiades.desc: A cluster of young blue stars, 440 light-years away, drifting through a dust cloud: their light reflects off it as a bluish veil.
observatory.orbitalis.body.proxima_b.des: The closest planet beyond the solar system, around a red dwarf. It lies where water could stay liquid, but its star's flares batter it relentlessly.
observatory.orbitalis.body.sagittarius_a: The black hole at the centre of our Galaxy, four million times the mass of the Sun. Nothing escapes it, not even light; around it, infalling gas glows, its light bent into a ring.
observatory.orbitalis.body.saturn.desc: The ringed planet: billions of blocks of ice, from grains to houses, in a sheet only a few tens of metres thick.
observatory.orbitalis.body.titan.desc: Saturn's great moon, under an orange haze thicker than our air. Methane rains down there, filling lakes and rivers. A parachute would almost be enough to land.
observatory.orbitalis.body.trappist_1e.d: One of seven Earth-sized planets circling a small, cool star. This one could hold oceans: a world to reach one day, at the end of a very long journey.
observatory.orbitalis.body.venus.desc: Earth's twin in size, and a hell: clouds of acid, 92 bar of pressure and 465 °C at the surface. No probe has lasted more than two hours there.
